items.summary: Home K Dissecting WerFault Henri Hambartsumyan This blog post documents the command-line parameters of WerFault.exe, obtained by reverse engineering the binary. Some inner WerFault workings are also discussed. A side note: I started this small side project in 2023. Reversing was, back then, still mostly a manual effort. Current AI tools can do this in a few minutes with probably more accurate descriptions, but I hope you can enjoy some artisanal reverse engineering. Introduction Modern Windows versions come with a large number of executables files. My system32 folder alone currently has 879 .exe files, while the wider C:\Windows has 5748 .exe files. However, only a small selection of those binaries have properties which are special and worth investigating. One of those binaries is WerFault.exe and its significant other WerFaultSecure.exe . There are two main reasons why WerFault is interesting from security perspective: It’s designed to create memory dumps and snapshots of other processes. There is limited documentation on the inner workings and command-line arguments. The first reason is interesting from an offensive perspective. Attackers can and do leverage WerFault. For example, to dump LSASS with “silentprocessexit”. But are there any other attack paths to leverage for offensive purposes? The second reason — limited documentation — is very annoying for detection engineering, incident triage and incident response purposes. I found a blog post from Helge Klein , which documents some things. Also, Hexacorn has a blog post on this topic , but in there are still unknowns which intrigue me. The best documentation I found so far was (of course 😉) the Windows Internals book. In this blog post, I’ll combine the information from the aforementioned three sources with knowledge obtained by reversing WerFault. Dispatching the call A logical place to start understanding the command-line argument is to start with the wmain function. Loading werfault.exe into IDA and loading the Microsoft-provided symbols, we can hit the ground running. Very quickly inside wmain you can see the parsing of the command-line arguments. Parsing the command-line arguments in wmain. And thanks to the symbols provided by Microsoft, we can already make out that the the first command-line option determines the “mode” of WerFault. Here, we notice a few things: The wmain function is a dispatcher. Based on the first command-line argument, it calls the corresponding “main” function. All the arguments are with a - except /hc and /h . Both /hc and /h do the same. All other command-line arguments are dependent on the specific function. The specific features, as suggested by the functions names, are also confirmed by the two blog posts mentioned earlier and the Windows Internals book. So far, so good. In the next sections, we’ll explore each of these functionalities individually. UserCrashMainSEH Based on the name, we can fairly assume that this function is invoked whenever a normal “user process” crashes. SEH in this context likely points to Structured Exception Handling . Looking again, the code is fairly easy to read in disassembled form, as well as in assembly. Here, we’re seeing again the parsing of the command-line arguments passed to UserCrashMain. Based on the error messages we can drive: -s refers to a shared memory handle. -p refers to the process id of the crashing process. -ip refers to a initiating process id. The relevant steps performed by this function: Parse and validate command-line arguments. -s is mandatory and -p are mandatory. -ip is optional. Open a handle to the process with pid -p . If -ip is set, open a handle to the process with pid -ip . Else open a new handle to the process with pid -p and use it as if it’s the initiation process id. Call WerpInitiateCrashReporting — as seen in screenshot below. A few things to note in this screenshot: XerDumpNotifyStart and XerDumpNotifyComplete are both imported from ext-ms-win-wer-xbox-l1-1-1.dll . This is a weird library I can’t find on any system I have access to. I’m also unsure what the relationship is with xbox. If you have any clue or have a copy of this binary, please let me know. Google only has 3 hits on this filename. There is nothing on VT. WerpInitiateCrashReporting is imported from faultrep.dll . There is plenty of things going on inside WerpInitiateCrashReporting , but we’ll skip that for now as it’s not relevant for the scope of this blog post. ReflectionServerMain This next function name doesn’t reveal much (to me) about what it does. Looking at the code, we see that this function only accepts one command-line argument with its corresponding value, being -pr XXXX . If the number of parameters provided is incorrect, it returns error code 0x80070057 , which translates to “ The parameter is incorrect ”. In the happy flow, we’re going to start the ReflectedDumpServer , passing in the value of the -pr argument — whatever that means. The value of the -pr is “The name of the file mapping object to be opened.” It’s passed to the lpName parameter of OpenFileMappingW . Based on the description of the workflow in the Windows Internals book Chapter 10, section “Windows Error Reporting”, I suspect the handle name passed to WerFault is the name of the shared memory object, potentially created by the crashing process. More debugging and reversing is required to confirm this. While following the decompiled code in IDA, it seems like the main goal of this mode ends up in a call to RtlCreateProcessReflection . This seems to be an undocumented function. However, there are plenty of details documented by all kinds of security researchers. Moreover, some details are described in “ Windows Internals, 6th edition, Part 2 ”. The latest edition (7th) doesn’t include this section. It’s a function which allows a process to be cloned. The function creates a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump , clones the process and “resumes” it. I suspect this is an attempt to restore a crashing process. But again, it requires more reversing to properly understand this. This is potentially a vector to either create a memory dump of LSASS directly or to clone LSASS with RtlCreateProcessReflection and then dump it. But this full attack chain is still unproven. WerCoreReportingHang Before diving into how this function works, note that in multiple ways this functionality feels like it’s been bolted on “after the fact”. First, there is the obvious difference in expecting command-line arguments with a / instead of a - . Next is the fact that it accepts two different command-line switches for the same function. All others have exactly one switch. Finally, the way the function is invoked is different. Consider the next screenshot from IDA. All functions take the full argc/argv pair, as passed to wmain , while a call to WerCoreReportHang strips the first command-line argument from argc/argv. The only command-line arguments which seems to be actually parsed in this function is the /SHARED argument. While based on actual process creation data in various environments, the /t and /p arguments seem to be passed. Either way, /p most likely refers to the process id again, while /t might refer to a thread id in case of a thread hang, but I can’t confirm this based on the code. As the function name suggest, this function is meant for error reporting on processes that are hanging. The first step is to check if the system has been configured to attach a debugger, based on HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\Hangs\Debugger . If a debugger is set, it executes the debugger. If applicable, it then waits until a debugger is attached and breaks. Next, it resets the PATH environment variable to the System32 folder, and sets a bunch more environment variables starting with _NT_. Then, it checks if a /SHARED argument is provided, which points to a shared memory object, just like earlier. If so, this shared memory is opened, copied locally and the structure is validated to see if it matches the undocumented type SharedHangRepData struct. We’ll skip most of the details of the next steps, but roughly the following happens: Initialize a CProcessInformation object containing the process id of the crashing process. Initialize a CHangReport object. Initialize a CUserModeHangReport object. Create the actual report by calling CHangReport::Create() . Submit the error report by calling CHangReport::Submit() . Obviously, this is an oversimplification, since a lot is happening , but the details are not very relevant for this blog post. SnapshotCaptureMain This mode, triggered by -pss , requires the same arguments as UserCrashMainSEH . -ip the initiating process id. -p the process id. -s a handle to a shared memory object. Note that here we’re dealing with a handle to the shared memory, opposed to a global name. The flow for this function is straightforward. Validate input. Open a handle to specified process ( -p ). Open a handle to specified initiating process( -ip ). If there is none, open a handle to same process as specified with -p . Make a snapshot of that process. The last step — creating a snapshot — is actually an interesting procedure, as it might offer some opportunities for LSASS dumping again. This does require some tinkering, as WerFault performs certain checks on the validity of the data in the shared memory section. Also it validates some other settings. For example, if the taking snapshots is allowed on the current system. The one thing which is still unclear to me, is how WerFault is supposed to MapViewOfFile , where the handle is directly a command-line argument and thus — by definition — external to WerFault. This is almost certainly related to shared memory sections, and the error reporting port which all Windows processes seem to have. SilentProcessExitMain This function is implemented as a proxy to the function WerUIReportSilentProcessExit in werui.dll . See the screenshow below. The implementation of SilentProcessExitMain in werfault.exe. Jumping into the implementation of this function in werui.dll , we see more weird things happening. It parses argc/argv looking for the following command-line arguments: -i The initiating process id. If the process is self-terminating, this is the same as the exiting process. If the silent process termination is triggered cross-process, this is the id of the process that started the termination. -e The exiting process. -t The thread id that sends the SilentProcessExit signal to WerFault. This is a thread id inside the process referenced by -i . -c The statuscode passed to ExitThread/TerminateThread. The table describing the registry entries “accidentily” documents this as well. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/debugger/registry-entries-for-silent-process-exit#monitor-process Since the details of how “Silent Process Exit” works are described in a lot of detail and the reversing didn’t reveal anything new, we won’t go into any more depth on this. KernelCrashMain KernelCrashMain handles both crash dumps and live kernel reports, so the name is a little misleading. It first parses the argument after -k to select an operation for this mode. The command-line options which determine the operation are: -c “Convert dump and report”. This operation processes an existing crash dump, queues the resulting kernel report and then attempts to report from the kernel queue. -q “Report from KQueue”. This operation skips the dump processing and starts working on reporting from the kernel queue directly. -l “Report live report”. Find and queue one live report into the KQueue. -lc “Convert live dump and report”. Process a full live dump and then submit it to WER. -lcq “Report all live reports”. This traverses the KQueue and submits each item to WER. Final remarks WerFault.exe is more than just a crash reporting utility. Depending on its command-line arguments, it can perform a variety of operations, including creating process snapshots, cloning processes, and generating memory dumps. Hopefully, this breakdown helps demystify some of WerFault’s less-documented behavior and provides a useful reference for analysts trying to distinguish legitimate activity from potential abuse.   • Both /hc and /h do the same. 

All other command-line arguments are dependent on the specific function. The specific features, as suggested by the functions names, are also confirmed by the two blog posts mentioned earlier and the Windows Internals book. So far, so good.

In the next sections, we’ll explore each of these functionalities individually.

UserCrashMainSEH

Based on the name, we can fairly assume that this function is invoked whenever a normal “user process” crashes. SEH in this context likely points to Structured Exception Handling.

Looking again, the code is fairly easy to read in disassembled form, as well as in assembly. 

Here, we’re seeing again the parsing of the command-line arguments passed to UserCrashMain. Based on the error messages we can drive:

  • -s refers to a shared memory handle.
  • -p refers to the process id of the crashing process.
  • -ip refers to a initiating process id.

 The relevant steps performed by this function:

  1. Parse and validate command-line arguments. -s is mandatory and -p are mandatory. -ip is optional.
  2. Open a handle to the process with pid -p.
  3. If -ipis set, open a handle to the process with pid -ip.
  4. Else open a new handle to the process with pid -p and use it as if it’s the initiation process id. 
  5. Call WerpInitiateCrashReporting — as seen in screenshot below.

A few things to note in this screenshot:

  • XerDumpNotifyStart and XerDumpNotifyComplete are both imported from ext-ms-win-wer-xbox-l1-1-1.dll. This is a weird library I can’t find on any system I have access to. I’m also unsure what the relationship is with xbox. If you have any clue or have a copy of this binary, please let me know. Google only has 3 hits on this filename. There is nothing on VT.
  • WerpInitiateCrashReporting is imported from faultrep.dll.

There is plenty of things going on inside WerpInitiateCrashReporting, but we’ll skip that for now as it’s not relevant for the scope of this blog post.

ReflectionServerMain

This next function name doesn’t reveal much (to me) about what it does. Looking at the code, we see that this function only accepts one command-line argument with its corresponding value, being -pr XXXX. If the number of parameters provided is incorrect, it returns error code 0x80070057, which translates to “The parameter is incorrect”.

In the happy flow, we’re going to start the ReflectedDumpServer, passing in the value of the -pr argument — whatever that means.

The value of the -pr is “The name of the file mapping object to be opened.” It’s passed to the lpName parameter of OpenFileMappingW. Based on the description of the workflow in the Windows Internals book Chapter 10, section “Windows Error Reporting”, I suspect the handle name passed to WerFault is the name of the shared memory object, potentially created by the crashing process. More debugging and reversing is required to confirm this. 

While following the decompiled code in IDA, it seems like the main goal of this mode ends up in a call to RtlCreateProcessReflection. This seems to be an undocumented function. However, there are plenty of details documented by all kinds of security researchers. Moreover, some details are described in “Windows Internals, 6th edition, Part 2”. The latest edition (7th) doesn’t include this section. It’s a function which allows a process to be cloned. The function creates a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump , clones the process and “resumes” it. I suspect this is an attempt to restore a crashing process. But again, it requires more reversing to properly understand this.

This is potentially a vector to either create a memory dump of LSASS directly or to clone LSASS with RtlCreateProcessReflection and then dump it. But this full attack chain is still unproven.

WerCoreReportingHang

Before diving into how this function works, note that in multiple ways this functionality feels like it’s been bolted on “after the fact”. First, there is the obvious difference in expecting command-line arguments with a / instead of a -. Next is the fact that it accepts two different command-line switches for the same function. All others have exactly one switch. Finally, the way the function is invoked is different. Consider the next screenshot from IDA.

All functions take the full argc/argv pair, as passed to wmain , while a call to WerCoreReportHang strips the first command-line argument from argc/argv. 

The only command-line arguments which seems to be actually parsed in this function is the /SHARED argument. While based on actual process creation data in various environments, the /t and /p arguments seem to be passed. Either way, /p most likely refers to the process id again, while /t might refer to a thread id in case of a thread hang, but I can’t confirm this based on the code.

As the function name suggest, this function is meant for error reporting on processes that are hanging. The first step is to check if the system has been configured to attach a debugger, based on HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\Hangs\Debugger. If a debugger is set, it executes the debugger. If applicable, it then waits until a debugger is attached and breaks. 

Next, it resets the PATH environment variable to the System32 folder, and sets a bunch more environment variables starting with _NT_. 

Then, it checks if a /SHARED argument is provided, which points to a shared memory object, just like earlier. If so, this shared memory is opened, copied locally and the structure is validated to see if it matches the undocumented type SharedHangRepData struct. 

We’ll skip most of the details of the next steps, but roughly the following happens:

  1. Initialize a CProcessInformation object containing the process id of the crashing process.
  2. Initialize a CHangReport object.
  3. Initialize a CUserModeHangReport object.
  4. Create the actual report by calling CHangReport::Create().
  5. Submit the error report by calling CHangReport::Submit().

Obviously, this is an oversimplification, since a lot is happening , but the details are not very relevant for this blog post. 

SnapshotCaptureMain

This mode, triggered by -pss, requires the same arguments as UserCrashMainSEH.

  • -ip the initiating process id.
  • -p the process id.
  • -s a handle to a shared memory object.

Note that here we’re dealing with a handle to the shared memory, opposed to a global name.

The flow for this function is straightforward.

  1. Validate input.
  2. Open a handle to specified process (-p).
  3. Open a handle to specified initiating process(-ip). If there is none, open a handle to same process as specified with -p.
  4. Make a snapshot of that process.

The last step — creating a snapshot — is actually an interesting procedure, as it might offer some opportunities for LSASS dumping again. This does require some tinkering, as WerFault performs certain checks on the validity of the data in the shared memory section. Also it validates some other settings. For example, if the taking snapshots is allowed on the current system.

The one thing which is still unclear to me, is how WerFault is supposed to MapViewOfFile , where the handle is directly a command-line argument and thus — by definition — external to WerFault. This is almost certainly related to shared memory sections, and the error reporting port which all Windows processes seem to have.

SilentProcessExitMain

This function is implemented as a proxy to the function WerUIReportSilentProcessExit in werui.dll. See the screenshow below.

The implementation of SilentProcessExitMain in werfault.exe.

Jumping into the implementation of this function in werui.dll, we see more weird things happening. It parses argc/argv looking for the following command-line arguments:

  • -i The initiating process id. If the process is self-terminating, this is the same as the exiting process. If the silent process termination is triggered cross-process, this is the id of the process that started the termination.
  • -e The exiting process. 
  • -t The thread id that sends the SilentProcessExit signal to WerFault. This is a thread id inside the process referenced by -i.
  • -c The statuscode passed to ExitThread/TerminateThread.

The table describing the registry entries “accidentily” documents this as well. 

Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/debugger/registry-entries-for-silent-process-exit#monitor-process

Since the details of how “Silent Process Exit” works are described in a lot of detail and the reversing didn’t reveal anything new, we won’t go into any more depth on this. 

KernelCrashMain

KernelCrashMain handles both crash dumps and live kernel reports, so the name is a little misleading. It first parses the argument after -k to select an operation for this mode.

The command-line options which determine the operation are:

  • -c “Convert dump and report”. This operation processes an existing crash dump, queues the resulting kernel report and then attempts to report from the kernel queue.
  • -q “Report from KQueue”. This operation skips the dump processing and starts working on reporting from the kernel queue directly.
  • -l “Report live report”. Find and queue one live report into the KQueue.
  • -lc “Convert live dump and report”. Process a full live dump and then submit it to WER.
  • -lcq “Report all live reports”. This traverses the KQueue and submits each item to WER.

Final remarks

WerFault.exe is more than just a crash reporting utility. Depending on its command-line arguments, it can perform a variety of operations, including creating process snapshots, cloning processes, and generating memory dumps.

Hopefully, this breakdown helps demystify some of WerFault’s less-documented behavior and provides a useful reference for analysts trying to distinguish legitimate activity from potential abuse.

items.title: How to Export FortiSIEM Logs
items.summary: Use FortiSIEM’s REST event query API. Post an XML query to /phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery, which returns a query ID, poll the progress until it reaches 100, then fetch the events. The results come back as XML. The original log line of each event is in the rawEventMsg attribute, so a few lines of Python turn the result into raw logs. Exports from the Analytics screen come out in formats LogTotal doesn’t read today. FortiSIEM is common wherever Fortinet runs the network, and it often holds far more than firewall logs. Prime Core has 19,692 detection rules for FortiSIEM, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API user. Use an account with rights to run analytics queries. The API authenticates with basic auth, with the organization in the username: super/ on an enterprise install, / for a specific organization in a service provider install. Retention. Online event storage is limited. Older events may sit in archive storage that needs extra steps. Attribute names. FortiSIEM queries use its own attribute names, such as reptDevName (reporting device), reptDevIpAddr, eventType and phRecvTime. Build the filter in Analytics first. Export with the event query API Save the query as query.xml: LogTotal export phRecvTime,reptDevIpAddr,eventType,rawEventMsg 1792368000 1792454400 reptDevName = "web-03" The interval is epoch seconds for 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. Then run it: FSM="https://fortisiem.example.com" AUTH="super/apiuser:$FSM_PASS" QID=$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' --data @query.xml "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery") until [ "$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/progress/$QID")" = "100" ]; do sleep 5; done curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/events/$QID/0/1000" > fsm_web03_1019.xml The last two path segments are the start offset and the count. Page through large results in steps of 1,000. Then pull out the raw messages: import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET root = ET.parse("fsm_web03_1019.xml").getroot() with open("fsm_web03_1019.log", "w") as out: for attr in root.iter("attribute"): if attr.get("name") == "rawEventMsg" and attr.text: out.write(attr.text.strip() + "\n") Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. What this looks like on real data. That’s what this FortiSIEM API speaks. The Python step converts it to the original raw lines, which is usually what you want to upload anyway. Can I export incidents instead? items.title: How to Export Graylog Logs
items.summary: Graylog keeps its messages in OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, so you have two routes. Use the Graylog REST API, authenticated with an access token, or query the backend indices (graylog_* by default) directly with a script. Either way you get JSON. The original line is in message, and in full_message for some inputs. The export in the Graylog web interface produces a format LogTotal doesn’t read today. Graylog is a popular open log management platform, often the first central logging a team sets up. Prime Core has 23,274 detection rules for Graylog, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get messages out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An access token. In Graylog, open your user’s settings and create a token. With the API, you authenticate as :token: the token as the username and the word token as the password. Backend access, if you go direct. The OpenSearch or Elasticsearch cluster behind Graylog often isn’t reachable from outside. Ask whoever runs it for a read-only account. Streams and index sets. Graylog routes messages into streams, and streams map to index sets with their own prefixes and retention. Know which index set holds your data. Option 1: Graylog REST API GL="https://graylog.example.com" curl -sS -u "$GL_TOKEN:token" -H 'Accept: application/json' -G "$GL/api/search/universal/absolute" \ --data-urlencode 'query=source:web-03' \ --data-urlencode 'from=2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z' \ --data-urlencode 'to=2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z' \ --data-urlencode 'limit=10000' \ | jq -c '.messages[].message' > graylog_web03_1019.jsonl Newer Graylog versions favor the Views search API. For large exports, Option 2 is more reliable. Option 2: Query the backend indices This is the same approach as our pointed at Graylog’s indices: import json, os from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers client = OpenSearch("https://opensearch.example.com:9200", http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]), verify_certs=True) query = {"query": {"bool": {"filter": [ {"term": {"source": "web-03"}}, {"range": {"timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19 00:00:00.000", "lt": "2026-10-20 00:00:00.000"}}}, ]}}} with open("graylog_web03_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="graylog_*", query=query, size=1000): out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n") Graylog stores timestamp as yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS in UTC, which is why the range uses that format. For a backend running Elasticsearch, use the elasticsearch client the same way. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 from the API Token auth written wrong Use :token 404 on the search endpoint Endpoint not available in your version Use Option 2, or the Views API Backend query returns nothing Wrong index prefix, or the timestamp format Check index sets; use yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS Backend not reachable Cluster not exposed Ask for read-only access, or use the API FAQ Message or full_message? Message is always there. full_message appears for some inputs, such as GELF, and can hold more detail. Export both if you have them. Does this work for Graylog Cloud? The API route does. Direct backend access usually isn’t available on hosted plans.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An access token. In Graylog, open your user’s settings and create a token. With the API, you authenticate as :token: the token as the username and the word token as the password.

Backend access, if you go direct. The OpenSearch or Elasticsearch cluster behind Graylog often isn’t reachable from outside. Ask whoever runs it for a read-only account.

Streams and index sets. Graylog routes messages into streams, and streams map to index sets with their own prefixes and retention. Know which index set holds your data.

Option 1: Graylog REST API 
GL="https://graylog.example.com"

curl -sS -u "$GL_TOKEN:token" -H 'Accept: application/json' -G "$GL/api/search/universal/absolute" \
  --data-urlencode 'query=source:web-03' \
  --data-urlencode 'from=2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z' \
  --data-urlencode 'to=2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z' \
  --data-urlencode 'limit=10000' \
  | jq -c '.messages[].message' > graylog_web03_1019.jsonl

Newer Graylog versions favor the Views search API. For large exports, Option 2 is more reliable.

Option 2: Query the backend indices

This is the same approach as our pointed at Graylog’s indices:

import json, os
from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers

client = OpenSearch("https://opensearch.example.com:9200",
                    http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]), verify_certs=True)
query = {"query": {"bool": {"filter": [
    {"term": {"source": "web-03"}},
    {"range": {"timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19 00:00:00.000", "lt": "2026-10-20 00:00:00.000"}}},
]}}}

with open("graylog_web03_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="graylog_*", query=query, size=1000):
        out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n")

  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review.

Message is always there. full_message appears for some inputs, such as GELF, and can hold more detail. Export both if you have them.

items.title: How to Export Wazuh Logs
items.summary: Wazuh keeps its data in two places. On the Wazuh manager, alerts are written to /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json, one JSON object per line, and rotated daily into compressed files by date. The same alerts are indexed in the Wazuh indexer (OpenSearch), in wazuh-alerts-4.x-*. Either way, the original log line that triggered an alert is in full_log. To export every event, not just the ones that matched a rule, the manager needs archiving turned on. Wazuh is the most widely used open-source SIEM and XDR, and its data is easy to get at once you know where to look. Prime Core has 23,542 detection rules for Wazuh, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to export alerts and events, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Alerts or archives? Alerts are the events that matched a Wazuh rule above the alert level threshold. Archives hold everything the manager received, but only if logall_json is enabled in ossec.conf. If the question is “what else happened on that host?”, you want archives, and they only exist from the moment they were turned on. Permissions. On the manager, the files are owned by the wazuh user and group, so use sudo. For the indexer, you need a user with read access to the alert indices. Retention. The manager’s rotated files stay until someone deletes them. The indexer keeps what its index lifecycle policy allows. Option 1: Files on the manager # today's alerts so far sudo cp /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json ./wazuh_alerts_today.jsonl # a past day (rotated and compressed) sudo zcat /var/ossec/logs/alerts/2026/Oct/ossec-alerts-19.json.gz > wazuh_alerts_1019.jsonl # one agent only jq -c 'select(.agent.name == "web-03")' wazuh_alerts_1019.jsonl > web-03_alerts_1019.jsonl # the original log lines behind the alerts jq -r '.full_log // empty' web-03_alerts_1019.jsonl > web-03_raw_1019.log With archiving enabled, the same pattern works for /var/ossec/logs/archives/archives.json and its rotated files under /var/ossec/logs/archives/ / /. Option 2: The Wazuh indexer The indexer is OpenSearch, so our applies as written. Point it at wazuh-alerts-* and filter on agent.name and timestamp: query = {"query": {"bool": {"filter": [ {"term": {"agent.name": "web-03"}}, {"range": {"timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}, ]}}} The Wazuh dashboard can also generate reports, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file: the alert JSON, or the raw lines from full_log. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Permission denied on the manager Files belong to the wazuh user Use sudo archives.json empty or missing logall_json isn’t enabled Enable it for the future; use alerts for the past No file for a past day Different rotation path or naming List /var/ossec/logs/alerts/ / / Some alerts have no full_log Not every alert comes from a log line (integrity checks, vulnerability detection) Upload the alert JSON instead Indexer returns 403 User lacks read access to wazuh-alerts-* Grant read on the alert indices FAQ Can I use the Wazuh API to export alerts? The Wazuh server API is for managing agents and configuration, not for searching alerts. Use the files or the indexer. Raw lines or alert JSON? Raw lines (full_log) when you want LogTotal to run its own detections on the original logs. Alert JSON when you also want Wazuh’s rule matches in the file.

Permissions. On the manager, the files are owned by the wazuh user and group, so use sudo. For the indexer, you need a user with read access to the alert indices.

items.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets and Steal Azure Key Vault Data in Just 5 Minutes
items.summary: Hackers are using the ARTEX AI framework to find exposed credentials on GitHub and turn them into access to cloud systems. In one observed case, an AI agent moved from searching public repositories for application secrets to stealing data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes, showing how quickly a coding mistake can become a cloud security incident. The operation combines credential hunting, automated analysis, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work from human operators. Instead of simply collecting leaked keys, the agents investigate what those keys can access and pursue valuable resources. The five-minute finding describes one documented case, not the time required for every attack involving the framework. Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Security Research identified the malicious activity in a November 5 report, tracing GitHub scanning to August 2026. Researchers described ARTEX as an offensive AI framework, rather than a conventional malware family. Earlier reporting on ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how agents interpret results and select subsequent actions, helping attackers connect familiar weaknesses faster. Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets The agents submitted large volumes of GitHub searches combining target organization names with terms associated with secrets, cloud platforms, and AI providers. Exposed material included application credentials and API keys for AI inference services. These searches target authentication data accidentally committed in scripts, configuration files, or other source code. Once useful credentials were found, agents obtained tokens for compromised OAuth applications and used their permissions to explore cloud resources. Microsoft observed agents extracting Azure Key Vault secrets and searching Azure DevOps for additional credentials. The wider problem of active GitHub credential exposure helps explain why this approach remains effective: publicly disclosed secrets can remain usable until their owners revoke or rotate them. In follow-on activity beginning as early as October 28, attackers used valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. Service principals, the identities applications use to authenticate, enabled access to dozens of applications across multiple tenants. Some compromised credentials belonged to vendor-owned multitenant applications, extending the risk to downstream customers. The attackers mapped subscriptions, permissions, resource groups, and AI deployments. They targeted storage keys, connection strings, App Service settings, publishing credentials, and Azure Kubernetes Service credentials. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain (Source – Microsoft) Compromised applications also accessed SharePoint and OneDrive, with observed file downloads and mailbox-item access. Agents additionally used Azure VM Run Command, a legitimate feature that can execute scripts inside virtual machines. The activity showed adaptive troubleshooting. After failed requests mixed Key Vault data-plane API versions with Azure Resource Manager control-plane endpoints, the agent retried approximately 28 seconds later using ARM version 2023-07-01 and received successful responses. Similar corrections followed failed Azure SQL and Application Insights requests. Such behavior supports the broader concern around autonomous AI credential theft , where automation can reduce delays between discovery and misuse. Detecting and Containing AI-Driven Cloud Credential Abuse Microsoft recommends treating publicly exposed credentials as compromised, even after developers delete the original code. Responders should revoke or rotate affected secrets, investigate historical use, and replace credentials stored in any Key Vault the compromised application could read. Disabling affected service principals may be necessary; already-issued tokens remain valid until expiry. Detection should connect identity events with subsequent cloud operations. Security teams should review Entra service-principal sign-ins, Azure Activity records, Key Vault diagnostics, storage logs, and Microsoft 365 audit data. One address accessing several service principals, or one application rapidly requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph, warrants investigation. IP matches alone should not determine attribution. Longer-term protection means reducing reliance on long-lived secrets through managed identities, enforcing least privilege, and enabling GitHub secret scanning and push protection. Microsoft also recommends monitoring secondary public repositories for leaked organizational credentials. Behavioral detections remain essential because attackers can change source addresses and user-agent strings, while legitimate tools can produce traffic resembling individual attack steps. items.title: CVE-2026-123158: OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass Affects Alpine Linux
items.summary: A high-severity vulnerability in OpenSSH can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to bypass password authentication on certain Linux systems by submitting an overlong password. Tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and dubbed SSHhole, the flaw carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and primarily impacts Linux environments where sshd is linked against musl libc and operates without PAM. Alpine Linux is the most prominent affected platform because its standard openssh-server package uses this configuration by default. The vulnerability results from an unexpected interaction between OpenSSH password validation and musl libc’s crypt() implementation. When an excessively long password is supplied, crypt() can return the string * to indicate an error. Some Linux accounts that are configured without a conventional password also store * in the password field of /etc/shadow. Under vulnerable conditions, sshd can incorrectly interpret the matching values as successful authentication. An attacker does not need to know the target user’s password. If an exposed SSH service meets the required conditions, an attacker who can reach the service can authenticate to certain accounts using a password in the vulnerable length range. The impact depends on the privileges assigned to the compromised account. Access to a privileged service account or an account capable of using doas or another privilege escalation mechanism could lead to full system compromise. Contact Sales OpenSSH addressed the issue in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2, released on November 5, 2026. Alpine Linux simultaneously released patched OpenSSH packages for all supported branches and several older branches. The OpenSSH team describes the release as containing a critical security workaround for Linux systems using musl libc with PAM disabled. Public reproduction environments and proof-of-concept material are already available. However, as of November 6, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks, and the flaw has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries and detection logic tailored to their available SSH, authentication, endpoint, and network telemetry. Detect CVE-2026-123158 by monitoring successful password-based SSH logins to accounts that normally use key-only authentication, unusual authentication attempts containing abnormally long passwords, unexpected remote access to service accounts, and post-authentication activity inconsistent with the account’s normal behavior. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-123158 analysis CVE-2026-123158 affects OpenSSH sshd before Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 when it runs on Linux with musl libc and password authentication occurs without PAM. The CVE carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, reflecting remote exploitation without prior privileges or user interaction but requiring a specific system and account configuration. The root cause lies in the interaction between OpenSSH and the password hashing function provided by musl libc. On systems where PAM is disabled, sshd performs password validation using the system’s crypt() functionality. For a typical account, /etc/shadow contains a cryptographic password hash, and the value generated from the user’s submitted password is compared against that stored hash. musl libc behaves differently when the supplied password exceeds its supported input length. For passwords longer than 256 bytes, crypt() returns * as an error value rather than a normal password hash. The problem arises because * is also commonly used in /etc/shadow for accounts that do not have a traditional password configured. If a vulnerable sshd receives an overlong password for one of these accounts, the authentication flow can effectively compare the * returned by crypt() with the * stored in the account’s shadow entry. The values match, and authentication can incorrectly succeed. The CVE description states that, for affected account configurations, passwords between 256 and 1024 characters can result in successful authentication. Independent reproductions describe passwords exceeding the normal 256-byte boundary as sufficient to trigger the vulnerable condition. The flaw is therefore not a universal password bypass affecting every OpenSSH deployment. Several specific conditions must align. First, the server must use musl libc. Alpine Linux is the primary mainstream example, although other embedded or minimal Linux environments can also use musl. Second, sshd must authenticate users without PAM. Alpine’s standard openssh-server package is built without PAM, while the alternative openssh-server-pam configuration is protected when UsePAM yes is enabled. Third, password authentication must be enabled. PasswordAuthentication yes is the relevant configuration. Systems configured for public-key-only authentication with PasswordAuthentication no are not exposed to the documented attack path. Finally, the attacker needs an account whose password field contains *. These can include key-only users, accounts created without passwords, some identities provided through directory services, and certain cloud-image users. Alpine also notes an additional condition: at least one local account must contain a $5$ or $6$-style password hash for the vulnerable authentication path to operate as described. The root account deserves special attention. Alpine commonly stores root:*, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password prevents password authentication directly to root. As a result, a standard Alpine installation does not automatically expose direct root login through this bug. That protection does not eliminate the broader risk. If another account with * in its password field is remotely accessible and has administrative rights through doas, sudo, container capabilities, or other privileged mechanisms, successful authentication can still provide a path to complete system compromise. Alpine’s official tiny-cloud images are particularly relevant. Security research identified versions where the alpine account could meet the vulnerable conditions and was also able to use doas to gain elevated privileges. This illustrates why defenders should evaluate account privileges rather than assuming the vulnerability provides either harmless user access or automatic root access in every environment. glibc-based Linux distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL are not affected by this specific vulnerability because the vulnerable behavior depends on musl libc’s password hashing implementation. Systems using PAM for SSH password validation are likewise outside the documented vulnerable configuration. Containers require similar qualification. Alpine is widely used as a container base image, but ordinary containers that do not run sshd are not vulnerable through this attack path. The primary concern is containers, appliances, development environments, or legacy workloads that explicitly install and expose an SSH server. The CVE-2026-123158 PoC landscape has developed quickly. Public reproduction labs are referenced directly by the vulnerability record, demonstrating that defenders should assume the authentication bypass can be reproduced without access to private exploit research. This materially raises remediation urgency even though confirmed malicious exploitation has not yet been reported. The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH publicly released version 10.6p2 with the security workaround on November 5, 2026. The reviewed primary sources do not specify the exact date on which the researcher initially discovered or privately reported the issue. The OpenSSH fix adds validation designed to prevent error values and invalid short password hashes from being accepted during password authentication. OpenSSH notes that it considers the underlying root cause to exist outside sshd, but because the condition can be exploited through the SSH server, the project implemented a defensive workaround in OpenSSH itself. Alpine Linux has backported the correction across multiple branches: Alpine branch Fixed OpenSSH package edge 10.6_p2-r0 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 3.18 9.3_p2-r4 3.17 9.1_p1-r7 3.16 9.0_p1-r6 Administrators should rely on their distribution package status rather than the SSH version banner alone. Linux distributions frequently backport security patches without changing the upstream OpenSSH version displayed during the SSH handshake. A server displaying an older version string may therefore already contain the vendor fix. For CVE-2026-123158 detection, defenders should prioritize SSH authentication telemetry. A particularly strong hunting signal is a successful password login to an account that is intended to use only public-key authentication or that has no usable password configured. On Alpine systems, administrators can review /var/log/messages, centralized authentication logs, SIEM records, or equivalent telemetry for Accepted password events involving unexpected service, key-only, or administrative accounts. Defenders should correlate successful authentication with source IP addresses, login times, session duration, commands executed after login, privilege elevation, changes to authorized_keys, account creation, scheduled jobs, and unexpected outbound network connections. Network telemetry can also help identify exposed systems. Externally reachable SSH services advertising password or keyboard-interactive authentication should receive higher remediation priority, particularly when the underlying system is Alpine or another musl-based distribution. At present, there are no campaign-specific CVE-2026-123158 IOCs such as confirmed attacker IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure. The absence of static indicators makes behavioral monitoring of SSH authentication and subsequent session activity particularly important. CVE-2026-123158 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the corrected package supplied by the Linux distribution. Alpine administrators should update the full system using the current package repositories and restart sshd afterward. Updating the package alone does not replace the already running SSH daemon process. Organizations running Alpine-based containers should rebuild and redeploy any image that installs openssh-server. Simply updating the host operating system does not patch vulnerable OpenSSH packages embedded inside container images. Administrators should also identify exposure before assuming that every Alpine host is vulnerable. Key checks include: Determine whether the host uses musl libc. Verify whether sshd is running with PAM disabled. Check whether password authentication is enabled. Identify login-capable accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is *. Review the privileges assigned to those accounts. Confirm the installed OpenSSH package against the distribution’s corrected package version. If immediate patching is impossible, organizations should disable SSH password authentication. Configure: PasswordAuthentication no and, where applicable: KbdInteractiveAuthentication no Administrators should confirm that public-key authentication works before applying this configuration to avoid losing legitimate administrative access. The SSH configuration should then be validated and the daemon reloaded or restarted. Afterward, external verification should confirm that the server offers only public-key authentication. Restricting network accessibility provides additional defense in depth. SSH should generally be reachable only from trusted administrative networks, VPN infrastructure, bastion hosts, or explicit source-IP allowlists rather than being universally exposed to the internet. Organizations should also reconsider whether SSH is required inside containers at all. Modern orchestration environments usually provide alternatives such as docker exec or kubectl exec, eliminating an unnecessary remotely reachable authentication service. For potentially exposed systems, review historical successful password logins occurring before remediation. Pay particular attention to accounts configured without passwords and identities normally expected to authenticate exclusively with SSH keys. If an unexpected successful login is identified, treat the account as potentially compromised. Review shell history where available, process execution, privilege escalation, new or modified authorized_keys entries, user and group changes, cron jobs, startup scripts, package installation, and outbound network connections. Credentials and keys accessible to the compromised account should be considered potentially exposed and rotated according to the findings of the investigation. If the account had administrative privileges, defenders should expand the investigation to the entire host and any systems reachable using credentials stored there. Public proof-of-concept material means organizations should not wait for evidence of widespread attacks before applying the fix. The exploitation prerequisites narrow the vulnerable population, but systems that meet those conditions can be accessed remotely without knowledge of a valid password. FAQ What is CVE-2026-123158 and how does it work? CVE-2026-123158 is a password authentication bypass affecting OpenSSH sshd on Linux systems using musl libc without PAM. When an excessively long password is passed to musl’s crypt() function, it can return * as an error value. If the target account also has * stored in /etc/shadow, vulnerable sshd configurations can incorrectly treat the values as matching and allow authentication. When was CVE-2026-123158 first discovered? The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH published the security fix in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, and the CVE became public the same day. The currently reviewed primary advisories do not disclose the exact date of the researcher’s original private discovery. What is the impact of CVE-2026-123158 on systems? Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to log in to a qualifying account without knowing its password. The resulting impact depends on that account’s permissions. Compromise of a service or standard account can expose data and application resources, while access to an account with doas, sudo, or equivalent privileges can potentially lead to complete system compromise. Can CVE-2026-123158 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Vulnerable OpenSSH installations remain exposed until patched or password authentication is disabled. The highest-risk systems are musl-based Linux environments such as Alpine Linux running sshd without PAM and containing qualifying passwordless accounts. Public reproduction material exists, although no confirmed exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 6, 2026. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123158? Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s patched package and restart sshd. If patching cannot be completed immediately, disable password and keyboard-interactive authentication, restrict SSH exposure to trusted networks, and review successful password logins for suspicious activity. Administrators should continue monitoring vendor advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-123158 as exploitation intelligence evolves.

Alpine also notes an additional condition: at least one local account must contain a $5$ or $6$-style password hash for the vulnerable authentication path to operate as described.

The root account deserves special attention. Alpine commonly stores root:*, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password prevents password authentication directly to root. As a result, a standard Alpine installation does not automatically expose direct root login through this bug.

That protection does not eliminate the broader risk. If another account with * in its password field is remotely accessible and has administrative rights through doas, sudo, container capabilities, or other privileged mechanisms, successful authentication can still provide a path to complete system compromise.

Alpine’s official tiny-cloud images are particularly relevant. Security research identified versions where the alpine account could meet the vulnerable conditions and was also able to use doas to gain elevated privileges. This illustrates why defenders should evaluate account privileges rather than assuming the vulnerability provides either harmless user access or automatic root access in every environment.

glibc-based Linux distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL are not affected by this specific vulnerability because the vulnerable behavior depends on musl libc’s password hashing implementation. Systems using PAM for SSH password validation are likewise outside the documented vulnerable configuration.

Containers require similar qualification. Alpine is widely used as a container base image, but ordinary containers that do not run sshd are not vulnerable through this attack path. The primary concern is containers, appliances, development environments, or legacy workloads that explicitly install and expose an SSH server.

The CVE-2026-123158 PoC landscape has developed quickly. Public reproduction labs are referenced directly by the vulnerability record, demonstrating that defenders should assume the authentication bypass can be reproduced without access to private exploit research. This materially raises remediation urgency even though confirmed malicious exploitation has not yet been reported.

The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH publicly released version 10.6p2 with the security workaround on November 5, 2026. The reviewed primary sources do not specify the exact date on which the researcher initially discovered or privately reported the issue.

The OpenSSH fix adds validation designed to prevent error values and invalid short password hashes from being accepted during password authentication. OpenSSH notes that it considers the underlying root cause to exist outside sshd, but because the condition can be exploited through the SSH server, the project implemented a defensive workaround in OpenSSH itself.

Alpine Linux has backported the correction across multiple branches:

Alpine branchFixed OpenSSH packageedge10.6_p2-r03.2410.3_p1-r23.2310.2_p1-r13.2210.0_p1-r113.219.9_p2-r13.209.7_p1-r63.199.6_p1-r33.189.3_p2-r43.179.1_p1-r73.169.0_p1-r6

Administrators should rely on their distribution package status rather than the SSH version banner alone. Linux distributions frequently backport security patches without changing the upstream OpenSSH version displayed during the SSH handshake. A server displaying an older version string may therefore already contain the vendor fix.

For CVE-2026-123158 detection, defenders should prioritize SSH authentication telemetry. A particularly strong hunting signal is a successful password login to an account that is intended to use only public-key authentication or that has no usable password configured.

On Alpine systems, administrators can review /var/log/messages, centralized authentication logs, SIEM records, or equivalent telemetry for Accepted password events involving unexpected service, key-only, or administrative accounts.

Defenders should correlate successful authentication with source IP addresses, login times, session duration, commands executed after login, privilege elevation, changes to authorized_keys, account creation, scheduled jobs, and unexpected outbound network connections.

Network telemetry can also help identify exposed systems. Externally reachable SSH services advertising password or keyboard-interactive authentication should receive higher remediation priority, particularly when the underlying system is Alpine or another musl-based distribution.

At present, there are no campaign-specific CVE-2026-123158 IOCs such as confirmed attacker IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure. The absence of static indicators makes behavioral monitoring of SSH authentication and subsequent session activity particularly important.

CVE-2026-123158 Mitigation

The primary remediation is to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the corrected package supplied by the Linux distribution. Alpine administrators should update the full system using the current package repositories and restart sshd afterward. Updating the package alone does not replace the already running SSH daemon process.

Organizations running Alpine-based containers should rebuild and redeploy any image that installs openssh-server. Simply updating the host operating system does not patch vulnerable OpenSSH packages embedded inside container images.

Administrators should also identify exposure before assuming that every Alpine host is vulnerable. Key checks include:

  1. Determine whether the host uses musl libc.
  2. Verify whether sshd is running with PAM disabled.
  3. Check whether password authentication is enabled.
  4. Identify login-capable accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is *.
  5. Review the privileges assigned to those accounts.
  6. Confirm the installed OpenSSH package against the distribution’s corrected package version.

If immediate patching is impossible, organizations should disable SSH password authentication.

Configure:

PasswordAuthentication no

and, where applicable:

KbdInteractiveAuthentication no

Administrators should confirm that public-key authentication works before applying this configuration to avoid losing legitimate administrative access.

The SSH configuration should then be validated and the daemon reloaded or restarted. Afterward, external verification should confirm that the server offers only public-key authentication.

Restricting network accessibility provides additional defense in depth. SSH should generally be reachable only from trusted administrative networks, VPN infrastructure, bastion hosts, or explicit source-IP allowlists rather than being universally exposed to the internet.

Organizations should also reconsider whether SSH is required inside containers at all. Modern orchestration environments usually provide alternatives such as docker exec or kubectl exec, eliminating an unnecessary remotely reachable authentication service.

For potentially exposed systems, review historical successful password logins occurring before remediation. Pay particular attention to accounts configured without passwords and identities normally expected to authenticate exclusively with SSH keys.

If an unexpected successful login is identified, treat the account as potentially compromised. Review shell history where available, process execution, privilege escalation, new or modified authorized_keys entries, user and group changes, cron jobs, startup scripts, package installation, and outbound network connections.

Credentials and keys accessible to the compromised account should be considered potentially exposed and rotated according to the findings of the investigation. If the account had administrative privileges, defenders should expand the investigation to the entire host and any systems reachable using credentials stored there.

Public proof-of-concept material means organizations should not wait for evidence of widespread attacks before applying the fix. The exploitation prerequisites narrow the vulnerable population, but systems that meet those conditions can be accessed remotely without knowledge of a valid password.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-123158 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-123158 is a password authentication bypass affecting OpenSSH sshd on Linux systems using musl libc without PAM. When an excessively long password is passed to musl’s crypt() function, it can return * as an error value. If the target account also has * stored in /etc/shadow, vulnerable sshd configurations can incorrectly treat the values as matching and allow authentication.

When was CVE-2026-123158 first discovered?

The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH published the security fix in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, and the CVE became public the same day. The currently reviewed primary advisories do not disclose the exact date of the researcher’s original private discovery.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-123158 on systems?

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to log in to a qualifying account without knowing its password. The resulting impact depends on that account’s permissions. Compromise of a service or standard account can expose data and application resources, while access to an account with doas, sudo, or equivalent privileges can potentially lead to complete system compromise.

Can CVE-2026-123158 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Vulnerable OpenSSH installations remain exposed until patched or password authentication is disabled. The highest-risk systems are musl-based Linux environments such as Alpine Linux running sshd without PAM and containing qualifying passwordless accounts. Public reproduction material exists, although no confirmed exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 6, 2026.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123158?

Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s patched package and restart sshd. If patching cannot be completed immediately, disable password and keyboard-interactive authentication, restrict SSH exposure to trusted networks, and review successful password logins for suspicious activity. Administrators should continue monitoring vendor advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-123158 as exploitation intelligence evolves.

items.title: Attacks on supermarket and blood storage systems prompt US warning
items.summary: Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough. On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk. On October 13, after the first attacks in France , refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network. A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised. Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken. CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles. The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware , and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits. What about home appliances? You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions. Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations. Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected. Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself. Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

items.title: After Binance, check what your signing systems can approve
items.summary: Binance’s October 2026 security incident raises an operational question for every organization holding user funds: Can your security controls recognize when a valid signature grants an attacker wallet authority? If an organization only monitors transfers and ownership changes, it may miss the shift in wallet authority until assets move. Binance’s initial update about the incident suggested that a compromised DevOps laptop allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. Its second update reported additional breaches but no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. In its November 3 report , Binance described a broader attack involving social engineering, misuse of an internal AI tool, stolen credentials, and unauthorized access to its wallet-signing service. The attacker nevertheless obtained valid signatures, illustrating a major risk: a compromised server with permission to request signatures can misuse a protected key without extracting it. The attacker used an EIP-7702 delegation that allows a wallet to sign a standing instruction: “Use this code when my account is called.” Ethereum keeps that instruction in place until it is changed or cleared using the wallet’s key. That enabled repeated transfers , including funds deposited after the first theft, without further signatures from Binance. Other Binance wallets were drained through ordinary signed transfers. Transaction execution and monitoring systems must keep pace with Ethereum. EIP-7702 places delegation authorizations outside ordinary calldata. Session keys, recovery paths, authorization modules, Safe modules, and ERC-4337 UserOperations all add execution paths that signing policies and monitors must understand. Systems that have not been updated can miss malicious authority changes and asset movements, leaving wallets exposed. Teams must update their detection rules and test that these attack paths are covered. If you’re responsible for securing wallet infrastructure, start with our checklist. Four steps to strengthen wallet security These four recommendations address the risks exposed by the attack. We also provide tests to help you verify that these security controls work. 1. Reduce access to signing infrastructure Document every service and API that can request wallet signatures, who can call it, and what it can authorize, including transfers, delegation, and arbitrary data. Review this inventory whenever wallet functionality changes on supported chains. Separate signing infrastructure from everyday business systems and verify transaction details through an independent system. Use our TRAIL method to trace how a compromised laptop or server could reach signing. Verify the result: For each identified compromise path, use the access and credentials available to the compromised system to attempt an unapproved action. Identify the control expected to block it and retain evidence that no usable signature was produced. 2. Treat delegation as an administrative privilege Configure signing services to recognize requests that change account authority. Reject EIP-7702 authorizations for custody externally owned accounts (EOAs) that do not need delegation, and ensure generic digest-signing APIs cannot bypass that restriction. Where delegation is required, separately approve the authorizing account, delegate address and code, chain, and nonce. Before evaluating execution, simulations must apply the proposed delegation and inspect changes to permissions and future execution authority alongside immediate balance changes. Verify the result: Delegation requests for accounts with delegation disabled are rejected through both dedicated and generic signing interfaces. Changing an approved account, delegate, chain, or nonce requires renewed approval. Simulations expose added authority even when the transaction moves no assets immediately. 3. Limit damage even if signing is compromised Even after delegation, the original EOA key can still transfer funds or change the delegate. This means that if the key is compromised, an attacker can bypass limits enforced by the delegate. Protect those assets with separate custody controls that the operational key cannot change. Our cold-storage guidance describes independently enforced limits, monitored delays on sensitive actions, and a separate configuration authority. Verify the result: Treat the operational key as compromised and attempt direct transfers, delegate replacement, and policy changes. Confirm these paths cannot bypass the claimed protections, including shortening or removing delays. Exercise incident response against a malicious withdrawal. Record alert and containment times, and demonstrate that responders can cancel or contain the withdrawal before execution. Confirm that the blocked withdrawal cannot subsequently execute. 4. Detect changes in wallet authority Map each wallet to the assets and contracts it controls, including wallets that hold no funds. Alerts should identify the affected systems and privileges (e.g., an unapproved delegation on an account that can upgrade funded vaults). Attribute direct calls, module execution, and ERC-4337 operations to their authorization paths. Verify the result: Test various delegation scenarios, mixed authorization tuples, multisig-module execution, and failed UserOperations inside successful bundles. Monitoring should reconstruct authority changes and asset movements in order, identify affected systems, and distinguish detection from controls that block execution before funds move. Make signing infrastructure an ongoing responsibility If your organization runs wallets or signing services, take another look at how they’re secured. Test whether your signing policies account for EIP-7702 and ERC-4337, whether independent safeguards still work if an attacker gains access to signing, and whether your monitoring catches changes to accounts and permissions. Give someone ownership of this review and put it on a regular schedule. Run it again whenever you change the protocols you support, the wallets you use, or your signing services.
