items.title: Faster LLM inference startup: What you need to know
items.summary: Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work. The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions. These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope. Why starting an inference server takes time A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve. Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance. The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay. What can be reused instead of rebuilt Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve: What is reused Approach Representative projects or features Work that can remain Model files Pre-staging and efficient loaders llm-d model caches, fastsafetensors Weight processing and initialization Compiled artifacts and tuning results Persistent caches vLLM compilation and autotune caches Runtime setup and graph capture Processed weights Daemons and weight transfer vLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpress Construction of the rest of the engine A live engine Sleep/wake and warm instances vLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMA Restoring released resources Initialized execution state Engine or container snapshots vLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKE Validation, restoration, and recovery work These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens. Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading , llm-d startup overview . What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation , preload documentation . This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node. vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode . A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots . SGLang SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation , Fast Engine Recovery roadmap . SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them. Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC , implementation PR . Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal , SGLang proposal . How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. Its operator and node agent coordinate CRIU and CUDA checkpoint operations, with resources such as PodSnapshot and SnapshotJob. Dynamo integrates these primitives into its serving workflows. Snapshot project . Snapshot’s documented storage path uses a shared persistent volume accessible by node agents. Agent-side components manage artifact movement and restore access. Its current storage documentation supports storage through a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC); object-storage backends are reserved for future use. Hardware, driver, runtime, and workload compatibility still constrain restoration. Storage model . The framework examples also show the application work involved. The SGLang example mounts an entrypoint that warms the engine, pauses generation, releases memory, and signals that capture is safe. After restoration, it resumes memory and generation, validates a generation, and starts its API. The vLLM guide validates its own entrypoint on v0.27.1 and explicitly says that example does not work on v0.28. This illustrates a compatibility boundary for that integration. SGLang guide , vLLM guide . Dynamo separately develops GPU Memory Service, which moves GPU-memory ownership outside the engine process. Its integration and snapshot support need to be read by version: Dynamo’s v1.4.0 Snapshot documentation explicitly describes GMS plus Snapshot as disabled and unsupported for production. GPU Memory Service , versioned Snapshot documentation . llm-d llm-d documents several startup approaches. Its Pod Snapshots guide currently covers single-GPU vLLM and SGLang deployments using GKE Pod Snapshots, GKE Sandbox based on gVisor, and Google Cloud Storage. The initial instance loads and warms the model, prepares its memory, and triggers a snapshot. Compatible later Pods restore that state and resume the framework. The guide describes a platform-independent CRIU backend as work in progress. Pod Snapshots guide . This backend differs from Snapshot’s CRIU path. gVisor saves sandbox state through its own checkpoint mechanism; GKE documents GPU-state capture through NVIDIA checkpoint support. Similar high-level workflows therefore do not imply identical checkpoint formats or APIs. GKE Pod snapshots . Fast Model Actuation takes another approach. It uses controllers and a requester/launcher Pod arrangement to manage vLLM instances. Depending on available state and placement, it can wake a sleeping instance or start one through a launcher that has already loaded Python modules. Its hot path depends on matching the retained instance to the assigned GPU. FMA guide . llm-d also documents ModelExpress for transferring weights from a seed replica to peers using NIXL and remote direct memory access (RDMA) over a compatible network. This changes weight distribution while leaving other engine-startup work to the receiving instance. These three paths illustrate why a platform’s startup work cannot be represented by a single checkpoint feature. ModelExpress integration . Where Kubernetes checkpoint and restore stands The Kubernetes Checkpoint Restore Working Group provides a place to coordinate use cases, API proposals, and integration with SIGs and runtimes. Its charter also identifies checkpoint archive efficiency as an area to revisit. The group’s scope concerns platform orchestration; inference frameworks continue to develop their internal startup mechanisms independently. Working-group charter . Kubernetes already has container checkpointing through the work associated with Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP) 2008, which reached beta in v1.30. KEP-5823 addresses Pod-level checkpoint and restore. It is marked implementable with a v1.38 alpha target; that milestone is a delivery target. Its initial boundaries exclude device state and cross-node restore. Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work.

The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions.

These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope.

Why starting an inference server takes time

A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve.

Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance.

The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay.

What can be reused instead of rebuilt

Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve:

What is reusedApproachRepresentative projects or featuresWork that can remainModel filesPre-staging and efficient loadersllm-d model caches, fastsafetensorsWeight processing and initializationCompiled artifacts and tuning resultsPersistent cachesvLLM compilation and autotune cachesRuntime setup and graph captureProcessed weightsDaemons and weight transfervLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpressConstruction of the rest of the engineA live engineSleep/wake and warm instancesvLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMARestoring released resourcesInitialized execution stateEngine or container snapshotsvLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKEValidation, restoration, and recovery work

These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens.

Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading, llm-d startup overview.

What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM

vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation, preload documentation.

This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node.

vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode.

A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots.

SGLang

SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation, Fast Engine Recovery roadmap.

SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them.

Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC, implementation PR.

Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal, SGLang proposal.

How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo

The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. Its operator and node agent coordinate CRIU and CUDA checkpoint operations, with resources such as PodSnapshot and SnapshotJob. Dynamo integrates these primitives into its serving workflows. Snapshot project.

Snapshot’s documented storage path uses a shared persistent volume accessible by node agents. Agent-side components manage artifact movement and restore access. Its current storage documentation supports storage through a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC); object-storage backends are reserved for future use. Hardware, driver, runtime, and workload compatibility still constrain restoration. Storage model.

The framework examples also show the application work involved. The SGLang example mounts an entrypoint that warms the engine, pauses generation, releases memory, and signals that capture is safe. After restoration, it resumes memory and generation, validates a generation, and starts its API. The vLLM guide validates its own entrypoint on v0.27.1 and explicitly says that example does not work on v0.28. This illustrates a compatibility boundary for that integration. SGLang guide, vLLM guide.

Dynamo separately develops GPU Memory Service, which moves GPU-memory ownership outside the engine process. Its integration and snapshot support need to be read by version: Dynamo’s v1.4.0 Snapshot documentation explicitly describes GMS plus Snapshot as disabled and unsupported for production. GPU Memory Service, versioned Snapshot documentation.

llm-d documents several startup approaches. Its Pod Snapshots guide currently covers single-GPU vLLM and SGLang deployments using GKE Pod Snapshots, GKE Sandbox based on gVisor, and Google Cloud Storage. The initial instance loads and warms the model, prepares its memory, and triggers a snapshot. Compatible later Pods restore that state and resume the framework. The guide describes a platform-independent CRIU backend as work in progress. Pod Snapshots guide.

This backend differs from Snapshot’s CRIU path. gVisor saves sandbox state through its own checkpoint mechanism; GKE documents GPU-state capture through NVIDIA checkpoint support. Similar high-level workflows therefore do not imply identical checkpoint formats or APIs. GKE Pod snapshots.

Fast Model Actuation takes another approach. It uses controllers and a requester/launcher Pod arrangement to manage vLLM instances. Depending on available state and placement, it can wake a sleeping instance or start one through a launcher that has already loaded Python modules. Its hot path depends on matching the retained instance to the assigned GPU. FMA guide.

llm-d also documents ModelExpress for transferring weights from a seed replica to peers using NIXL and remote direct memory access (RDMA) over a compatible network. This changes weight distribution while leaving other engine-startup work to the receiving instance. The group’s scope concerns platform orchestration; inference frameworks continue to develop their internal startup mechanisms independently. Working-group charter.

KEP-5823 addresses Pod-level checkpoint and restore. It is marked implementable with a v1.38 alpha target; that milestone is a delivery target. Its initial boundaries exclude device state and cross-node restore. GPU support has a separate provisional proposal, KEP-6274, whose enhancement PR remains open and discusses device allocation and compatibility. items.title: Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws to Hide Fileless Backdoor and Launch Ransomware Attack
items.summary: A China-linked threat group tracked as Storm-2603 has used the SharePoint ToolShell flaws to plant a backdoor that never touches the disk. The group then tried to run Warlock ransomware on the same network. The break-in hit an on-premises SharePoint server and ended with a ransomware launch that security software blocked. ToolShell is the name for a set of Microsoft SharePoint bugs, including CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771. They let an attacker run code on a server through specially crafted web requests. Microsoft linked the ransomware side of this activity to Storm-2603, while other groups using the same flaws mostly stole data and spied. Defenders who thought July 2025 patching closed the story should note that unpatched servers were still being hit months later. Researchers at Securelist , the threat research arm of Kaspersky, identified and documented this intrusion in a report published on November 5, 2026. Their team found the activity in a December review of a customer’s logs. They noted that the attackers kept control inside the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, and wrote nothing to disk for the backdoor itself. You can read the full Securelist analysis for the technical details. Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws The first sign was small. On December 20, a single request hit a SharePoint ToolPane endpoint to check whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770. It came from infrastructure tied to ONYPHE, an internet scanning platform. About 12 minutes later, a second connection arrived from a bulletproof hosting provider, Pfcloud UG. Nothing was exploited yet, and three quiet days followed. Because of that gap, the team first rated the probe as low priority. The real intrusion came on December 24, Christmas Eve, when many security teams run with fewer staff. Attack chain (Source – Securelist) The attacker sent a crafted request from 45.91.94[.]204, a Safing Privacy Network node that hides the true source behind several relays. That request loaded a webshell straight into the IIS worker process. It ran in memory and vanished if the application pool was recycled or IIS restarted. This matches what earlier reports on the ToolShell zero-day and Warlock ransomware warned about. The webshell was a modular C# framework. Its main part, G.cs, registered a custom VirtualPathProvider, which lets ASP.NET serve pages that do not exist as files. It woke up only when a request carried a specific User-Agent, so normal traffic never triggered it. It talked to the attacker over a custom binary protocol with simple XOR scrambling. It also used the suo5 proxy tool to tunnel traffic through the SharePoint host, which let the attackers reach other machines inside the network. Other modules listed running processes, logged-on users and network connections. One installed MSI packages silently, and another created admin accounts through low-level Windows account calls instead of normal commands. For SYSTEM rights, the code used a named-pipe trick copied from the EfsPotato tool, which works because IIS worker processes hold the needed impersonation privilege. Velociraptor, Tunnels and a Blocked Warlock Launch Soon after the webshell ran, the worker process started msiexec.exe to install a package from Supabase cloud storage. The package was Velociraptor version 0.73.4.0, a real forensics tool with a known flaw, CVE-2025-6264. Cisco Talos had already described Velociraptor abused in ransomware cases tied to the same group. Here, the attackers used it for persistence, discovery, data collection and running payloads. Through Velociraptor, they set up several backup routes: Zoho Assist, VS Code tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel and a small reverse proxy. With so many paths, deleting one tool would not end their access. They also stopped depending on the webshell or the ToolShell bug at this point. The group then dropped a vulnerable driver, rsndispot.sys, to shut down endpoint protection. Fingerprinting with ONYPHE (Source – Securelist) A sideloaded DLL, flagged as Warlock’s antivirus killer, was likely meant to use it. This fits earlier findings on custom malware that abuses BYOVD from the same actor. The final step failed. Kaspersky’s Proactive Defense Module blocked the Warlock ransomware process before it could encrypt anything. Securelist assigns the case to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, based on the ToolShell use, the Warlock tools and the Velociraptor habits. For defenders, patching is not enough. Install Microsoft’s emergency SharePoint security updates , then rotate exposed MachineKeys and hunt for persistence. Watch for odd w3wp.exe behavior, new VirtualPathProvider registrations, unexpected outbound connections and new remote-management tools. Securelist also advises keeping memory and IIS logs, and treating a confirmed exploit as a full host compromise. items.title: Huntress turns real-world attack intelligence into fleet-wide ‘herd immunity’ with new platform capabilities
items.summary: Huntress has announced a wave of new capabilities across its Agentic Security Platform, designed to turn intelligence gathered from live attacks into proactive defences for every customer, rather than leaving each incident as one organisation’s problem. The updates span Managed ITDR, Managed EDR, Managed SIEM, Managed SAT and Managed ISPM. They draw on the company’s visibility across nearly 300,000 businesses, 17 million identities and 6 million endpoints, combined with its 24/7 AI-centric Security Operations Center (SOC). The principle is simple: when an attack targets one organisation, Huntress applies what it learns across its entire fleet through automated blocking, earlier detection of hidden compromises, attack disruption and real-time user interventions. “Defending against threats moving at machine speed requires knowing the adversary better than anyone else and anticipating their next move by continuously learning from every attack and leveraging our scale and elite security researchers to turn that intelligence into stronger protection,” said Prakash Ramamurthy, Chief Product Officer at Huntress . “These innovations demonstrate how we’re bringing together unrivaled human expertise, AI, and real-world threat intelligence to protect businesses at the speed adversaries operate.” Blocking identity attacks at sign-in The headline addition to Managed ITDR is Adversary Infrastructure. When Huntress confirms hosting, relay or proxy infrastructure being used in an identity attack, it converts that intelligence into a blocking Conditional Access policy across every eligible, opted-in Microsoft 365 tenant the same day. One customer’s incident becomes protection for the wider customer base before the attacker can move on to the next target. Managed ITDR also now detects and shuts down suspicious service principals. The feature builds on Huntress’ investigation into the ConnectWise/SkyKick vendor compromise, in which attackers used stolen vendor credentials to access Microsoft 365 environments. It analyses service principal sign-ins, issues detailed incident reports and automatically disables compromised applications without partner intervention. It is available now for tenants with Microsoft Entra ID P1 licensing or higher. A third ITDR feature, Lookback, reviews up to 180 days of login history for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. It looks for evidence of credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers and data centre logins that predate deployment. Where a compromise is still active, Huntress investigates and revokes the affected identity’s sessions. During early access, Lookback helped an MSP uncover a compromised $2 million real estate wire transfer, with suspicious activity dating back three days before onboarding. Disrupting remote ransomware Huntress says nearly 30% of the ransomware cases it observed this year originated from an unprotected system, which attackers use as a foothold for reconnaissance and to launch attacks across the network. Because these remote attacks leave few conventional indicators on protected endpoints, they are hard for traditional endpoint tools to stop. Managed EDR now uses Ransomware Canaries to detect this activity and automatically block communication between protected systems and the compromised, unprotected machine, stopping the spread. The capability becomes generally available on 30 November and activates automatically on systems protected by Managed EDR. Brute force visibility and identity posture Brute Force Sentry, a new Managed SIEM capability, detects brute-force activity across Windows RDP, RD Gateway, RDWeb and Linux SSH, correlating failed sign-ins with subsequent successes across log sources. items.title: ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers, Some Hosting Cyberattack Tools
items.summary: Security researchers have found ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, exposed on 1,465 internet-facing hosts. Some servers also hosted command-and-control tools, phishing software, and exploit files, showing how automated security-testing platforms are appearing alongside established attack infrastructure. The findings offer defenders a view of these environments, including files operators left publicly accessible. The count does not mean 1,465 separate hacking groups are operating the framework. Around 650 hosts shared repeated configurations across two hosting providers, suggesting cloned systems or servers using multiple addresses. Removing those clusters leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments. Public exposure also does not establish malicious activity, because authorized security testers can use ARTEX. Researchers from Censys identified the exposed consoles and associated attack tools in a November 5 report. They described ARTEX as a dual-use framework, not a malware family. Their investigation found additional threat detections on 155 hosts, or 10.6% of the total, and 32 open directories exposing tools, implants, and operator files. ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers Released on July 26, 2026, ARTEX combines a Go backend, Next.js console, and PostgreSQL database. It connects with ScopeSentry, an asset-discovery platform, to import domains, addresses, ports, and endpoints. Operators define a target, testing scope, and objective; AI agents then plan tasks, execute tools, and record results. Earlier coverage of ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how this approach reduces manual work across attack stages. A planner breaks objectives into smaller actions, while worker agents run tools such as nmap and return findings. ARTEX maintains an asset graph showing discovered systems and an exploration graph tracking what has been tested. ARTEX’s workflow (Source – Censys) It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, and compatible model endpoints, allowing operators to change providers without rebuilding the workflow. Censys found CyberStrikeAI alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts, with PentAGI, HexStrike AI, and RedAmon also appearing. Other servers carried Vshell, Cobalt Strike, Adaptix C2, FRP, and Gophish. These combinations matter because reconnaissance, phishing, remote access, and AI-assisted testing can sit together, although shared hosting alone does not prove a coordinated attack. The exposed directories provided stronger operational clues. Their contents included Windows lateral-movement tools, a public sudo exploit, Linux implants, reverse-shell scripts, and compiled stagers. One directory exposed One directory exposed an operator’s home folder, including SSH material and shell history. Separate reporting on ARTEX Active Directory attacks describes how agents have supported credential attacks and movement between Windows systems. Censys also traced an ARTEX server cited by CrowdStrike to open directories visible from August 18, seven weeks before CrowdStrike’s report. That investigation linked ARTEX to attacks against South Korean financial institutions. Separately, Microsoft attributed ARTEX-assisted activity against ConnectWise customer tenants to Storm-0940. Coverage of ARTEX Microsoft 365 targeting details that campaign’s scanning, password spraying, and OAuth abuse. Defenders should correlate infrastructure matches with authentication logs, endpoint activity, and network connections rather than treat every ARTEX console as hostile. Censys recommends checking nearby open directories, tunneling services, unfamiliar LLM gateways, and historical scan records. Short-lived directories are particularly useful: ten disappeared and fifteen appeared elsewhere between November 3 and November 5. items.title: Claude Dispatch Flaw Lets Malicious Browser Extensions Run Code on Connected Computers
items.summary: A flaw in Anthropic’s Claude Dispatch let a malicious browser extension run commands on a computer via Claude Desktop. That computer could even be a different machine signed into the same Claude account. Researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security named the technique ThisBash and published the findings on November 4, 2026. Anthropic plans to retire Dispatch, but the design behind it still lives in other Claude features. Dispatch lets a person send a task from a phone to Claude Desktop, an AI agent that can work with local files, apps, and commands. Anthropic’s help page says the feature is in limited beta and is closed to new users. The same page warns that a manipulated instruction could trigger actions that are hard to undo. The researchers found no flaw in the phone-to-desktop link itself. The trouble started when the same workflow was reached from claude.ai in a browser, where an extension can run alongside the page. Claude Dispatch Vulnerability Claude Desktop is an Electron app. That means it is built from the same web interface and API as claude.ai. The web version only hid the Dispatch link. It never blocked access to it. Once someone copied the page address from the desktop app, any logged-in browser tab could open Dispatch and send requests. An extension with permission to run scripts on claude.ai could do the same through the user’s own cookies. In the proof of concept , the script opened Dispatch in a tiny 200 by 200 pixel background window. It then asked the API for the session ID of the user’s desktop agent. This was the only visible trace on screen. Claude first hesitated when asked to install an unknown npm package. The script read each reply and sent a follow-up in the user’s voice. Forever Security calls this prompt forcing. In normal prompt injection, hostile text hides inside a page or file that the model reads, and the attacker gets one try. In prompt forcing, the attacker controls the whole chat and can rephrase, insist and try new angles until the model gives in. Four written prompts were enough. A short loop also clicked any “Allow” button once per second, so no human had to approve anything. The package then ran and opened Calculator. The team noted that the same step could have copied files, added SSH keys or planted a backdoor. Dispatch is built to link devices, so the browser and the desktop do not need to be on one computer. Picture an employee who signs into a personal Claude account on a work laptop. A bad extension in their home browser could then send orders to that work laptop. It would run next to source code and cloud keys. The researchers said they have seen personal accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on at corporate endpoints. Extensions are common enough to make this a real path. LayerX found that 99% of enterprise users in its sample had at least one extension, and 53% had extensions with high or critical permissions. Forever Security’s earlier MaXSS and Spyder research showed how flaws in two popular Chrome extensions, with over 10 million installs between them, could let websites act across other sites. A bad extension can come from a rogue install, a hijacked update or a bug in a trusted tool. A malicious extension can already read pages, steal data and act through logged-in sessions. That is serious. But it normally stays inside the browser. ThisBash crossed that line. Permission to talk to a website became permission to run commands on the computer. The requests also looked real. They came from a real session and a real account, with permissions the user had granted. That proved who was logged in. It did not prove the user wanted a command to run. The researchers put it this way: a web session alone is not proof that the user approved an action on their machine. Researchers have shown extensions steering AI tools several times this year. Cyber Security News covered BragJack , where a single extension took over the built-in assistants of five major browsers. That story shows the problem goes well beyond one vendor. Any AI tool that trusts the page it sits in can be steered by code running in that page. Weizman reported the issue to Anthropic on May 14, 2026. Anthropic confirmed it was valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of a problem it had already found. On October 13, the company said Dispatch would be retired, with a target of the end of October 2026. That date has now passed, and I could not confirm from public sources that the feature is fully gone. The wider concern is that Claude Code Remote Control and Cowork sessions let the web drive a local agent by design. The researchers say extensions can repeat the same trick there and plan a follow-up post. Taking away one feature does not remove the trust gap underneath. Start with a list of the AI agents on your endpoints and the accounts they use. Check whether those accounts sit under company single sign-on. Turn off cross-device remote control where there is no business need, and review how devices are paired and removed. Treat extensions like any other software. Limit who can install them, review their permissions and watch for updates that ask for more. Approval prompts should be something the requesting component cannot click for itself. Teams should also watch for odd package installs, config changes and credential access linked to agent activity. Anthropic recently added a beta EDR monitoring option for Claude Cowork on Team and Enterprise plans, which can help with that last step. The simplest habit is also the strongest. Keep personal AI accounts off work devices, and keep work accounts out of personal browsers. ThisBash shows why that line matters. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Hackers Could Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Steal Conversations Without Users Knowing
items.summary: A flaw in ChatGPT let attackers slip past Lockdown Mode, the safety setting meant to stop data leaks. Check Point Research found that a hidden pop-up trick could copy a user’s full chat history, show fake windows, and push malware. In the ChatGPT Classic desktop app, simply chatting was enough to trigger the leak. OpenAI has fixed the bug. OpenAI launched Lockdown Mode on February 13, 2026, first for business plans. On June 4, it reached personal accounts, where users can turn it on under Settings > Security. The setting limits web browsing to cached pages and turns off live web access, image support in replies, Deep Research, Agent Mode, Canvas networking, live connectors, and file downloads. OpenAI says it is built for high-risk users, such as executives and security teams, and is not needed by most people. Our earlier story on the ChatGPT Lockdown Mode release covers the basics. The goal is to stop prompt injection, where hidden text tricks the AI into following an attacker’s orders. A common trick is to make the AI load a link like attacker.example/collect?data= followed by private details. The data then shows up in the attacker’s server logs and the chat looks normal. ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass This is not the first hidden exit path Check Point has found. In March, the team showed that DNS tunneling in ChatGPT’s code runtime could send chat data to an outside server. We covered that bug in ChatGPT Vulnerability Let Attackers Silently Exfiltrate User Prompts . The new flaw shows how closing one path does not protect the others. In February 2026, OpenAI added an HTML preview to ChatGPT code blocks, so users can view a page right in the chat. That page runs inside two nested iframes, which are small boxed-in web pages. The box blocks outside images, scripts, and links, and it asks the user before anything leaves. Researcher Alexey Bukhteyev spotted a weak point. The boxes allowed popups through two settings, allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox. ChatGPT guarded popups by swapping out the window.open function. A page could skip that guard by adding one more iframe and calling that iframe’s own window.open. The popup then opened with no prompt, even in Lockdown Mode. Since the second setting was on, code in the popup ran outside the box. The first risk was fake update windows. The popup kept the ChatGPT icon, while the attacker chose the title. That made a malware download look like a real app update. In a browser, downloads are not blocked, so a shared chat link was enough, and the victim did not even need an account. In the desktop app, the user still had to click the download link. The second risk was silent data theft. In ChatGPT Classic, built on Electron, window.open worked without any user click. A malicious prompt, a malicious custom GPT, or a shared chat could then send the whole conversation, and uploaded files, to the attacker’s server. The third risk was stolen logins. The team also reloaded the main ChatGPT window and signed the user out. A fake login page could then capture the password when the user signed back in. Check Point reported the problem to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI said it removed both popup permissions from the outer preview iframe. Check Point retested and confirmed the trick no longer works. Check Point published its report on November 5. No user action is needed for this specific bug, but a few habits lower the risk of similar ones. Do not click buttons, previews, or “update” prompts inside shared chats. Skip prompts copied from unknown sites and avoid custom GPTs from unknown builders. Check the address bar or sign-in page before typing a password, especially after an unexpected logout. Keep the desktop app updated, and avoid pasting medical, financial, or work secrets into any chat unless needed. Even OpenAI says its safeguards reduce risk but give no full guarantee. As AI tools run code and show web content, each new feature adds a new way in. Careful habits remain a necessary layer of protection. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. The goal is to stop prompt injection, where hidden text tricks the AI into following an attacker’s orders. A common trick is to make the AI load a link like attacker.example/collect?data= followed by private details. The data then shows up in the attacker’s server logs and the chat looks normal.

ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass

This is not the first hidden exit path Check Point has found. In March, the team showed that DNS tunneling in ChatGPT’s code runtime could send chat data to an outside server. We covered that bug in ChatGPT Vulnerability Let Attackers Silently Exfiltrate User Prompts. The new flaw shows how closing one path does not protect the others.

In February 2026, OpenAI added an HTML preview to ChatGPT code blocks, so users can view a page right in the chat. That page runs inside two nested iframes, which are small boxed-in web pages. The box blocks outside images, scripts, and links, and it asks the user before anything leaves.

Researcher Alexey Bukhteyev spotted a weak point. The boxes allowed popups through two settings, allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox. ChatGPT guarded popups by swapping out the window.open function. A page could skip that guard by adding one more iframe and calling that iframe’s own window.open.

The popup then opened with no prompt, even in Lockdown Mode. Since the second setting was on, code in the popup ran outside the box.

The first risk was fake update windows. The popup kept the ChatGPT icon, while the attacker chose the title. That made a malware download look like a real app update. In a browser, downloads are not blocked, so a shared chat link was enough, and the victim did not even need an account. In the desktop app, the user still had to click the download link.

The second risk was silent data theft. In ChatGPT Classic, built on Electron, window.open worked without any user click. A malicious prompt, a malicious custom GPT, or a shared chat could then send the whole conversation, and uploaded files, to the attacker’s server.

The third risk was stolen logins. The team also reloaded the main ChatGPT window and signed the user out. A fake login page could then capture the password when the user signed back in.

Check Point reported the problem to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI said it removed both popup permissions from the outer preview iframe. Check Point retested and confirmed the trick no longer works. Check Point published its report on November 5.

No user action is needed for this specific bug, but a few habits lower the risk of similar ones. Do not click buttons, previews, or “update” prompts inside shared chats. Skip prompts copied from unknown sites and avoid custom GPTs from unknown builders.

Check the address bar or sign-in page before typing a password, especially after an unexpected logout. Keep the desktop app updated, and avoid pasting medical, financial, or work secrets into any chat unless needed.

Even OpenAI says its safeguards reduce risk but give no full guarantee. As AI tools run code and show web content, each new feature adds a new way in. Careful habits remain a necessary layer of protection.

items.title: Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting for Public Apps to Prevent Unauthorized Admin API Access
items.summary: Shopify is making IP allowlisting mandatory for public apps that call its Admin API, adding a security check to limit the use of stolen access tokens. Developers must enable the control by November 20, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET. Apps using bulk operations face an earlier deadline of November 12 at the same time. The change turns a security feature introduced on October 27 into a requirement. Shopify will check where API requests come from, rather than relying on a valid token alone. This addresses the risk covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s cloud API security guide , where stolen credentials can give attackers access to cloud services. Once allowlisting is active, Shopify checks the source IP of GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests using the app’s tokens. Requests from outside approved addresses or networks receive an HTTP 403 response. Shopify also rejects requests when it cannot confirm the source address. Apps that miss the November 20 deadline face removal from the Shopify App Store and blocked new installations. Existing installations can continue operating until April 1, 2027, when Admin API requests will fail. However, bulk queries and mutations face the earlier November 12 cutoff. Merchants will receive admin warnings from January 15. The policy targets token misuse, a risk illustrated by Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on the Internet Archive’s repeated breach through unrotated API tokens . Network restrictions add protection, but developers still need to secure their credentials. An attacker operating inside an approved network could remain within the permitted boundary. Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting Shopify’s setup guide supports specific public IP addresses and address ranges for static infrastructure. Apps with changing addresses can approve hosting networks through autonomous system numbers, or ASNs. Developers can list up to 10 ASNs and narrow access to up to 10 countries. These network rules are broader than individual server addresses. Developers configure the control under Settings in the Dev Dashboard and test it against recent traffic before enabling enforcement. Shopify recommends checking whether legitimate requests would be blocked, then confirming an outside request fails. Apps must choose either IP addresses or networks, because saving one type replaces the other. Shopify’s official announcement lists November 12 in its detailed bulk-operation instructions, despite November 11 appearing in its summary. Separately, public apps must migrate to expiring offline tokens by January 1, 2027, adding time limits alongside network restrictions. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Microsoft Paint 0-Click Vulnerability Could Allow Hackers to Take Control of Windows PCs
items.summary: Microsoft’s Windows Paint vulnerability, CVE-2026-83844, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code over a network without user interaction. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.1, placing it in the High severity category rather than Critical. However, confusion over the corrected Paint version has complicated patch checks for Windows administrators. The vulnerability stems from an out-of-bounds read, a memory error in which software reads beyond its intended boundary. Microsoft published the advisory on October 13, 2026. Its assessment lists a network attack vector, no required privileges, and high attack complexity, meaning successful exploitation depends on conditions that make an attack harder to carry out. Windows 0-Click Paint RCE Vulnerability The disclosure formed part of the October update cycle, covered in Cybersecurity News’ Microsoft October Patch Tuesday report . For administrators, the immediate concern is not simply whether an update exists, but whether the corrected application build has actually reached managed devices. Microsoft initially listed Paint version 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed release. Administrators reported that Microsoft Store continued offering 11.2605.81.0, even after update checks and Store cache resets. Microsoft’s advisory listed 11.2609.401.0 as the fix, suggesting the earlier version reference may have been incorrect. Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation. Update availability also appears inconsistent. Some administrators reported difficulty obtaining a corrected build, while one participant in the Reddit discussion said the update had become available through Microsoft Store. These individual reports do not establish a universal rollout status. Claims that availability depends on region also remain unverified. A crafted image could trigger the flaw, but Microsoft’s quoted guidance describes a crafted network packet sent to an affected service. The Hacker News discussion highlights the missing detail: neither the exposed service nor the complete attack path is identified. Suggestions involving Copilot or other components are speculation. Administrators should check the installed Paint version rather than trust an “up to date” message alone. Neowin recommends following Microsoft’s current advisory and considering temporary removal where Paint is unnecessary. Restricting untrusted images may reduce general exposure, but it is not a confirmed fix for this specific network attack path. Cybersecurity News’ separate PNG vulnerability coverage provides related context on image software security. Those flaws are separate from this Paint vulnerability. items.title: Groklem: an Android banker that rents Grok to read your texts
items.summary: A bank OTP lands on a phone somewhere in South Asia. Before the owner has even glanced at it, a background service has copied the message, scraped the last ten days of their texts to go with it, and shipped the bundle off with one instruction: find the money . Seconds later an answer comes back, not to the victim, but to a stranger on the other end of a socket: a tidy JSON summary of the victim’s bank accounts, their latest balance, and a guess at what’s in there right now. OTPs, card alerts, PIN resets, all sorted and labelled. The thief never read a single text himself.
